key_finding: A nudge that shrinks the visibility of the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cuts minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but does not significantly reduce debt, because nudged cardholders opt for autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and some drop out of autopay entirely, raising missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts with six-month follow-up, comparing nudged vs. control cardholders' autopay enrollment and payment behavior.
why_it_matters: This is direct evidence for the support team's 'vanity enrollment' worry in a genuinely consumer, self-directed financial product: a choice-architecture nudge changed nominal behavior without changing the substantive outcome (debt paid down), which is exactly the enrollment-vs-amount distinction the round-up feature decision turns on.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
nudge shrouded an option rather than setting a full opt-out default
relevance_reason: Closest consumer-financial-product evidence that enrollment metrics can diverge sharply from the amount-level outcome the feature is meant to produce.

key_finding: A state-of-the-art narrative overview of DC plan design concluding that automatic enrollment and default investment options raise participation but can carry negative effects on participant engagement, with effects moderated by framing and communication.
methodology: Narrative literature overview; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides a broad map of the pension-default literature's current concerns (engagement costs, framing) but stays inside the employer-plan setting the brief says does not transfer directly.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
no effect sizes given in the abstract
overview rather than primary evidence
relevance_reason: Background synthesis of the analogous employer-pension literature the brief flags as relevant by analogy only.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces long-run passivity (low contribution rates, inattentive account management, account churn), so participation alone is insufficient evidence of welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative policy commentary; abstract-only, no original data reported.
why_it_matters: States plainly, in commentary form, the same 'enrollment is not welfare' argument the support team is making, reinforcing that headline enrollment numbers should not be the success metric.
limitations: US retirement plan context, not consumer app
no quantitative effect sizes
low-citation, non-empirical commentary
relevance_reason: Explicit articulation of the passive-enrollment risk the brief asks us to weigh against the default-enrollment upside.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when and how default effects persist or fade downstream, identifying time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as the key moderators of long-run default effects.
methodology: Conceptual review and framework synthesis of the consumer-default literature; no new primary data.
why_it_matters: Gives the project a structured way to predict which of our two design choices (entry, level) is likely to show a lasting vs. fading effect, and why enrolled-but-disengaged users are a documented, theorized pattern rather than an anecdote from support.
limitations: conceptual synthesis, not a quantitative meta-analysis
no numeric effect sizes to anchor design decisions
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: The review-level synthesis the brief asks for on whether and how default effects persist versus decay, in a genuinely consumer (non-employer) framing.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option, even when it causes substantial losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments in Medicare Part D, including one with random assignment to default options.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that default persistence and passivity insensitivity are general phenomena beyond retirement plans, useful for calibrating how strong an effect we might see, but the setting (public health insurance) is far enough from a liquid consumer savings app that it caps as supporting rather than decisive evidence.
limitations: health-insurance domain, not financial savings
beneficiaries are older/low-income Medicare population, not a general banking-app user base
relevance_reason: Shows default passivity can persist strongly regardless of stakes, informing how sticky our chosen default might be — but off the brief's specific setting.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6 percentage points from automatic enrollment and 0.3 points from default auto-escalation once job separation, unvested-balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out are accounted for; only 40% of those defaulted into auto-escalation follow through on the first scheduled increase.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, withdrawal-on-separation, and auto-escalation opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: The single strongest quantified rebuttal to the 'defaults will lift enrolment, so default everyone in' argument: it shows the true steady-state effect of automatic enrollment/escalation is far smaller than headline participation-rate lifts suggest, directly undercutting the internal case for full opt-out enrollment.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-plan mechanics (vesting, job separation) don't map onto a banking app
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving amounts, which the brief explicitly asked us to test.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most affected individuals actively opted out, and the default effect was stronger when incentives were higher and knowledge of enrollment status was lower.
methodology: Administrative and survey data analysis around a nationwide auto-enrollment policy rollout.
why_it_matters: Quantifies how much default strength depends on incentive salience and awareness — relevant to predicting whether a round-up default will actually stick versus be reversed by aware users, though the setting is a mandatory public pension, not a discretionary consumer feature.
limitations: public pension system with government-mandated enrollment, not a consumer app
'most opt out' finding may reflect pension-specific stakes rather than general default weakness
relevance_reason: Gives a concrete default-effect size and shows dependence on incentive salience and knowledge, informing how strong our default is likely to be perceived.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, are attenuated by 36 months; average savings increases are modest at the longer horizon, though inequality in savings is significantly reduced, and a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Empirical analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: This is the closest available quantified answer to the brief's central persistence question — does the default effect on enrolment survive past sign-up — showing attenuation over time even in the closest available analogous literature, which should temper expectations for the round-up feature's 6-12 month enrolment numbers.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a self-directed consumer app
life-cycle model calibrated to retirement savings, not small liquid round-ups
relevance_reason: Provides the most directly quantified estimate of default-effect attenuation over medium-run horizons, the closest prior work on the persistence question the brief asks about.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (especially one people refuse) lowers users' rating of the advice/wealth manager, an effect mediated by perceived honesty; question framing in the default presentation also shifts chosen allocations.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, manipulating default presence and framing of investment defaults.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the EU-consumer-relevant reputational cost of defaults — a default that people override actively damages trust — which bears squarely on whether an opt-out round-up default will read as helpful or manipulative, and on how the preset multiplier should be framed to avoid an anchoring/dark-pattern read.
limitations: wealth-management investment-allocation context, not a round-up savings app
advisor-mediated setting differs somewhat from a purely self-service app flow
relevance_reason: The only EU-context experimental evidence quantifying when a default is perceived as manipulative, and how framing of the default level shifts chosen amounts — bears directly on both the entry and level decisions.

key_finding: In three firms with automatic 401(k) enrollment, participation exceeded 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the default 2-3% savings rate and default conservative fund, and half remained at the default rate/fund even after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms analyzing automatic-enrollment participation, default contribution rate, and default fund adherence over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that people anchor heavily on preset contribution levels — directly relevant to whether a preset round-up multiplier will anchor users at that level rather than the level they would otherwise choose — but the brief explicitly discounts this era of pension work as the setting has since changed.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, not a consumer app
no year given in metadata; a decades-old classic study now superseded by more recent replications in this set
no exploration of liquid/withdrawable savings behavior
relevance_reason: The foundational study behind the 'preset level anchors contribution choice' finding that later, more recent papers in this set build on and revise.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together (friction complementarity), and adding an extra menu option captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on large-scale transaction data, validated with a stated-preference survey; counterfactual menu-design simulation.
why_it_matters: Offers a mechanism-level account of why defaults 'stick' (ease of opting out matters as much as preference alignment), which could inform how we design the exit/opt-out flow, but the tipping-menu setting and lack of any financial-savings framing keep it at background relevance.
limitations: tipping decisions on taxi rides, not a financial savings product
no persistence or enrollment-rate outcomes analogous to the brief's questions
relevance_reason: A methodologically rigorous decomposition of default-adherence mechanisms that could inform opt-out friction design, but in an unrelated consumer setting.

key_finding: In an opt-in short-term (withdrawable-anytime) savings program at five UK firms, at most 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account, but among those who did, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution 12 months later.
methodology: Field study of program rollout and account activity at five UK employers, tracking activation and 12-month account balances/contributions.
why_it_matters: The closest available real-world analog to the round-up feature itself — a liquid, withdrawable, opt-in savings product — showing the exact trade-off the brief asks about: opt-in produces very low take-up but strong sustained engagement among those who join, directly informing the entry-mode decision.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction channel, not a standalone banking app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice arms in the same study
relevance_reason: Directly matches the product type (liquid, withdrawable, opt-in short-term savings) and quantifies the low-uptake/high-persistence trade-off central to the entry decision.

key_finding: Characterizes asymptotically optimal default rules: when designer and chooser agree on the activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions to cases of disagreement and externalities.
methodology: Theoretical characterization of optimal default policy with numerical simulations validating asymptotic approximations; abstract-only beyond that.
why_it_matters: Offers general normative principles for choosing a default (e.g., minimize opt-out when designer and user interests align) that could inform which round-up multiplier to preset, but it is abstract theory without any grounding in a financial-app or consumer population.
limitations: purely theoretical with simulated validation, no empirical population studied
not tailored to financial products or liquid savings
relevance_reason: General theory of optimal default design relevant to choosing which multiplier to pre-set, but disconnected from any concrete consumer-financial evidence.

key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, arguing EU regulation of pre-selected defaults and similar choice-architecture practices is fundamentally about protecting consumer autonomy.
methodology: Doctrinal/legal analysis of EU consumer-protection law; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the legal-risk side of the opt-out vs active-choice decision: gives the specific criteria EU regulators use to judge whether a pre-selected enrollment default crosses into a sanctionable autonomy violation.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence on enrollment or amounts saved
no data on our specific product category
relevance_reason: Provides the EU regulatory framework for judging whether opt-out enrollment or a pre-selected multiplier would read as a dark pattern, which the brief flags as a reputational risk.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (vs. ~50% under lower defaults), and many stayed at a rate below the employer match threshold and below what their income would predict.
methodology: Administrative retirement-plan data, single large 12% default plan compared against a literature review of lower defaults; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Strongest direct evidence that a pre-set level anchors people at a value that may be worse for them than an unconstrained choice — a caution for setting the pre-selected round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer app
no employer-intermediary analogy for our product
relevance_reason: Best available quantified evidence on default anchoring at a specific preset level, directly analogous to the multiplier pre-selection question even though the setting is a pension plan.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted/unavailable ('Trant'), so no usable finding can be extracted beyond the title's claim of four large UK payroll-savings automation experiments.
methodology: abstract-only (text not retrievable); title indicates field experiments on payroll savings automation.
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant given the same author team's other automatic-enrollment work, but with no readable content it cannot presently inform any decision.
limitations: abstract not available, no extractable data
payroll savings still involves an employer-linked mechanism, not a consumer app
relevance_reason: Same research group's related automatic-savings work, but unusable in its current form.

key_finding: At-scale field experiments at major UK banks show automatic enrollment into just-in-time text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though alerts captured less than half of potential avoidable savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments across major UK retail banks; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for opt-out enrollment inside an existing consumer banking app: it quantifies both the size of the behavior-change benefit and its shortfall relative to full potential, which is exactly the trade-off the enrolment-default decision needs measured against.
limitations: overdraft alerts, not a savings/round-up feature
no explicit 6-12 month persistence breakdown given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Directly on-point: UK retail-bank consumer product, opt-out/auto-enrollment mechanism, quantified real behavioral and monetary effects, not an employer-mediated setting.

key_finding: Over 41 months, automatic pension enrollment raised average savings by £32-38/month but also raised unsecured debt by £7/month and mortgage balances by £118, partially offsetting the savings gain, while also modestly improving credit scores.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment across ~160,000 UK employers with 2-29 employees; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Shows that a default-driven savings increase can be partly illusory once offsetting financial behavior is accounted for — a caution against treating enrollment or even nominal savings totals as the success metric without checking net financial position.
limitations: employer-sponsored pension, not a liquid consumer savings feature
no data on withdrawal/disengagement in a self-directed app context
relevance_reason: Directly tests the brief's concern that defaults may inflate nominal savings numbers without real net benefit, in a large well-powered natural experiment.

key_finding: Adding a minor 'ordeal' step (removing auto-enrollment) reduced health insurance enrollment by 33%, differentially excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people, undermining the standard rationale that ordeals screen out low-value enrollees.
methodology: Natural policy experiment studying removal of an auto-enrollment default in a public health insurance program, plus a selection-market model; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Warns that adding friction (an opt-in-like 'ordeal') to save on low-value sign-ups can instead strip out exactly the vulnerable users the feature is meant to help — relevant to weighing opt-in against opt-out for a savings feature.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a savings product
no employer or fintech analogue in the abstract
relevance_reason: Directly informs the distributional risk of adding friction to enrollment (relevant to opt-in vs. active choice trade-offs), though in a different market.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on 2020 US campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who likely did not intend a recurring commitment.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across multiple political campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring-donation boxes at different times; observational/quasi-experimental.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world evidence that a pre-checked recurring-contribution default can lift nominal sign-up while simultaneously generating regret and complaints in the least-experienced users — precisely the support team's objection, quantified.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
refund requests are a proxy for regret, not a direct complaint or withdrawal metric
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise with a large quantified estimate of both benefit and consumer detriment, plus the exact heterogeneity (inexperienced, small users) the brief asks about.

key_finding: In a search model with reference-dependent utility, defaults raise the reservation utility (helping choosers who accept them) while self-selection means those who reject the default are more likely to find superior options; both effects are confirmed experimentally.
methodology: Laboratory choice-with-search experiment testing a formal reference-dependent search model; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: General theoretical mechanism for why defaults help some and not others, but too abstract and domain-generic to directly inform the enrolment or level decisions.
limitations: generic lab search task, no financial or app context
no measure of enrollment persistence or amount saved
relevance_reason: Background theory on why defaults create heterogeneous benefit, relevant to the distributional question but not decision-specific.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects sustained at least 15 months, showing active choice screens can meaningfully shift default-driven behavior.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered EU DMA choice-screen rollout across iOS and Android; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether a mandated active-choice screen (the exact 'active choice' onboarding design under consideration) produces large, persistent behavior change relative to a preset default, in an EU regulatory context comparable to ours.
limitations: browser default, not a financial savings product
no individual-level enrollment/engagement or complaint data
relevance_reason: The closest empirical evidence on whether forced active choice meaningfully changes outcomes relative to defaults, under the same EU regulatory regime the product will operate in.

key_finding: A 'generalizable active privacy choice' interface applying one opt-out decision across many sites made opting out far less disruptive (98% of participants felt undisrupted for the best scheme, a 40-point improvement) while only slightly reducing opt-out utility, in a 410-participant usability study.
methodology: Usability study of nine opt-out interface schemes implemented in a browser extension; N=410; experimental.
why_it_matters: Offers a concrete UX pattern — generalizing one active choice across many instances — for reducing the friction cost of forced active choice, relevant to designing an active-choice onboarding screen that doesn't feel burdensome.
limitations: privacy consent context, not a financial savings feature
law here bars default opt-out, a stricter regime than our legal clearance
relevance_reason: A methods precedent for making forced active choice less disruptive, which bears on how to implement (not whether to implement) active choice onboarding.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-up uptake, but for outcomes requiring real effort (exam preparation, passing), gains appeared only among individuals already responsive to university communication; non-responsive individuals showed increased nominal sign-up with no effect on the effortful target outcome.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up defaults across university programs, with heterogeneity analysis by past responsiveness; experimental.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the mechanism the support team worries about: a default lifts nominal sign-up numbers without lifting the effortful behavior actually needed, and the split depends entirely on who is targeted — a template for predicting which round-up enrollees will actually engage.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial product or app
heterogeneity measured via past university responsiveness, not a directly transferable segmentation for banking customers
relevance_reason: Best available demonstration that opt-out enrollment can inflate nominal enrollment while leaving effort-dependent outcomes unchanged for less-engaged individuals, the core 'vanity metric' concern in the brief.

key_finding: After target-date funds became the default retirement investment option under the Pension Protection Act, younger and older workers' stock allocations diverged in line with the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little following the policy.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of US middle-class investors, 2006-2018; observational.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can strongly anchor an allocation-type choice (like which multiplier level) while leaving the underlying contribution amount largely unaffected — a caution that a preset multiplier default might anchor the setting without changing how much people actually save.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not liquid consumer savings
default is an investment glidepath, not a round-up multiplier
relevance_reason: Relevant evidence that defaults can anchor a parameter choice (multiplier-like) without moving the deeper outcome (amount saved), directly bearing on the anchoring question.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with default-option and positive-narrative nudges producing the largest backfire, and effects varying by income, education, gender, and financial motivation.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions; N=220.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving: here the default option nudge backfires and lowers willingness to contribute, with heterogeneity by demographic group that mirrors the brief's distributional concern.
limitations: hypothetical/survey-based willingness rather than real enrollment behavior
small sample (N=220) and a different cultural/regulatory context (China, not EU)
pension savings context rather than liquid round-up savings
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in this batch that a default can actively reduce rather than raise contribution intentions, satisfying the brief's explicit request for a contradicting paper.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, financial nudges were rated neutral-to-positive on approval, benefit and ethics regardless of transparency or messenger, with strong preference for System 2 (reflective) interventions and saving-framed messages over spending-framed ones.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment with 36 hypothetical financial intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting; representative Australian sample.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether a bank-originated default or nudge reads as helpful or manipulative to consumers, which is exactly the reputational risk the brief flags for an EU opt-out design and should shape how the round-up default is framed and disclosed.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not a real product decision
Australian sample, not EU
measures stated approval/perception, not actual enrolment or savings behaviour
relevance_reason: Most direct evidence in this batch on whether consumers perceive financial defaults as manipulative versus helpful, bearing on C5's dark-pattern risk.

key_finding: Offering CCT recipients a choice between bank deposit or cash had no significant average effect on overall savings, but raised balances for those who previously held nonpositive balances.
methodology: Field experiment with conditional cash transfer beneficiaries; experimental evidence on delivery channel choice.
why_it_matters: Shows a channel-choice intervention can be a null result on average while helping a specific subgroup, a caution against treating enrolment numbers as a proxy for savings impact.
limitations: subsidy delivery channel choice, not an enrolment default in a savings feature
developing-country CCT population, not EU consumer banking app users
relevance_reason: Weakly analogous evidence that a savings-adjacent choice architecture change can fail to move aggregate savings despite subgroup effects.

key_finding: Abstract fragment describes an automatic-enrollment IRA with an emergency-savings feature where liquid-fund amounts and benefits are identical across compared cases.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to be a program-evaluation table description, no clear design details available.
why_it_matters: Touches the liquid-emergency-savings-plus-default theme close to a round-up feature, but the abstract gives no usable effect size or comparison.
limitations: abstract is uninformative/truncated, no effect sizes or method visible
national IRA policy context rather than a bank app feature
relevance_reason: Topically adjacent (auto-enrollment IRA with liquid savings) but too thin to be actionable evidence.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and a large fraction of automatically enrolled employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation ('default' behaviour) even though almost no opt-in employees had chosen that combination.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment on 401(k) plan design change within one large US corporation, administrative enrollment and contribution data.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset default doesn't just raise sign-up but anchors the level people end up at — the exact mechanism decision 2 (preset multiplier) worries about — but it is an employer-mediated retirement plan, so it caps out as background rather than actionable evidence for this consumer app.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, not a self-directed consumer app
no 6-12 month withdrawal/disengagement data
no distributional/manipulation analysis
relevance_reason: Classic prior work establishing default anchoring on contribution level and fund choice, the closest precedent to the level-anchoring question, but off-domain for a consumer product.

key_finding: No abstract available; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviours between automatic and voluntary enrolment in a defined contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only, unknown design.
why_it_matters: Potentially another auto- vs voluntary-enrolment comparison but cannot be assessed without content.
limitations: no abstract text to evaluate claims or effect sizes
retirement plan setting, not a consumer app
relevance_reason: Topically on-target title but no extractable evidence.

key_finding: Across three representative Estonian surveys, low institutional trust and minority (non-Estonian) status predicted both under-saving and early withdrawal from a pension scheme after an early-withdrawal option was introduced.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of three nationally representative surveys (2020-2022) around an Estonian pension reform introducing early withdrawal.
why_it_matters: Identifies exactly the kind of distributional harm the brief worries about — those already saving too little are also most likely to disengage/withdraw — a caution against assuming a default-enrolled cohort is uniformly helped.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme, not a liquid consumer app
no data on enrolment defaults themselves, only withdrawal correlates
Estonia-specific institutional context
relevance_reason: Directly relevant to who is helped versus hurt by enrolment and withdrawal dynamics, informing the distributional/manipulation-risk criterion, though set in a pension context.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, being prompted to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrollment vaccine booster policy reduced stated vaccination intentions and decreased approval of the policy, contrary to expectation.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment (n=24,303) across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a default-enrollment policy.
why_it_matters: Direct empirical evidence that making a default salient can backfire and reduce support/behavioural intent — a warning for opt-out design that if the default becomes visible or discussed (as EU disclosure norms may require), it could provoke backlash rather than passive acceptance.
limitations: vaccination policy context, not financial savings
measures stated intentions in a hypothetical scenario, not actual enrolment or savings behaviour
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in this batch that a default, once reflected upon, can reduce rather than increase engagement/support — directly pushes against the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment and employer matching provisions were associated with higher likelihood of retirement plan participation among US Millennials in the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study.
methodology: Cross-sectional regression analysis of survey data (FINRA 2018 Millennial Investment Study).
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the well-established auto-enrollment participation lift in a younger cohort but adds little beyond stronger existing evidence (e.g. Madrian & Shea, Choi et al.) and is employer-plan specific.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
correlational survey design, no causal identification
no persistence, anchoring, or distributional analysis
relevance_reason: Redundant confirmatory evidence on auto-enrollment participation lift, replaceable by stronger causal studies already in the portfolio.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, each $1 of tax-subsidy expenditure raised total saving by only 1 cent because 85% of people are 'passive savers' unmoved by subsidies but heavily influenced by automatic contributions, while the 15% who are 'active' mainly shift assets across accounts rather than saving more.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis (Denmark, ~41 million observations) exploiting variation between active-choice subsidy policies and automatic/passive contribution policies.
why_it_matters: The strongest available evidence that a default changes real accumulated wealth for the majority who are passive, not merely who is nominally enrolled — directly answers the brief's question of whether defaults change the amount saved versus just enrolment counts, and shows the effect is concentrated among the financially less sophisticated, informing who is helped.
limitations: government retirement/tax-advantaged accounts in Denmark, not a self-directed liquid consumer app
the employer/state-as-intermediary trust mechanism the brief flags as non-transferable may partly drive the passive-saver result
no data on withdrawal or disengagement of passive savers
relevance_reason: Uniquely detailed evidence distinguishing nominal enrolment from real savings impact across active/passive saver types, the closest existing answer to the brief's central 'vanity metric' question.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision, no default) and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option can motivate behaviour change as a complement or alternative to automatic enrollment when opt-out defaults are infeasible or unethical.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against no-intervention/default baselines, building on Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick's active-choice framework.
why_it_matters: This is the primary source for the 'active choice' design option itself, directly informing whether forcing a yes/no answer at onboarding can capture most of the enrolment benefit of opt-out without its ethical/manipulation downsides — the exact trade-off decision 1 is weighing.
limitations: field experiments largely in medication-adherence contexts rather than financial products
no long-term (6-12 month) persistence or withdrawal data reported
abstract does not give quantitative effect sizes for the enhanced active choice condition
relevance_reason: The originating method/design precedent for active choice as an alternative to opt-out defaults, the mechanism central to the entry-design decision (C6).

key_finding: This NBER handbook chapter synthesises household finance evidence on savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and surveys interventions including choice architecture, product design, and default effects used by firms and governments to shape financial behaviour.
methodology: Narrative literature review/handbook chapter (Beshears, Choi, Laibson, Madrian).
why_it_matters: Provides the broad review-level synthesis of choice-architecture effect sizes and mechanisms across household finance that the brief explicitly asks for, giving a check on whether single-study estimates generalise before the round-up feature is built.
limitations: narrative overview, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
covers many domains at a high level rather than round-up savings specifically
abstract-only detail on which parts concern consumer defaults versus employer plans
relevance_reason: The review/synthesis needed in the evidence portfolio to check single-study default effect estimates against the broader household-finance literature.

key_finding: Across three large firms, automatic enrollment pushed 401(k) participation above 85%, but about 80% initially accepted both the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default conservative fund, and half of participants were still on the default rate and fund after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large US firms comparing pre/post automatic-enrollment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The most quantitatively detailed evidence available on whether a preset level anchors people at that level and whether this persists over years rather than fading — directly bears on whether shipping a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor most users there long after signup.
limitations: employer 401(k) context, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
measures retirement contribution/fund choice anchoring, not a round-up multiplier
no explicit engagement/complaint or withdrawal-rate data
relevance_reason: Strongest and most detailed evidence on default-level anchoring and its multi-year persistence, the closest analogue to the preset-multiplier decision despite the employer setting.

key_finding: In a randomized field experiment in Afghanistan, default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% matching incentive — driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives, and it increased later active saving after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment assigning employees to different default configurations of a salary-linked savings account, with follow-up interventions to isolate mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Offers a rigorous, mechanism-focused estimate of default effect size and evidence that default assignment can shift subsequent active saving behaviour even after removal, informing whether default enrolment could have lasting positive effects beyond mere nominal sign-up.
limitations: salary-linked savings account tied to employment, not a self-directed consumer banking app
Afghan employee population, very different context from EU consumers
no multi-month withdrawal or disengagement/complaint data reported
relevance_reason: Strong causal estimate of default effect size and its psychological mechanisms, useful context though set in an employer-linked, non-EU environment.

key_finding: A reminder nudge in a Brazilian consumer financial app reduced credit-card late fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%, with a net 5% fee increase for users with a history of overdraft use while other users saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform (Brazil), comparing fee outcomes between nudged and control users, with subgroup analysis by overdraft history.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern that a well-intentioned intervention can help most users while harming a vulnerable subgroup — the exact distributional risk the team must check before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level presets
outcome is fee incidence, not savings enrolment or amount saved
Brazilian credit-card context differs from EU round-up savings regulatory setting
relevance_reason: Strongest available RCT evidence that a nudge can produce net harm for an identifiable subgroup even while helping the average user, bearing directly on the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk question (C5).
